title: High-affinity hemoglobin (low P50): compensatory erythrocytosis
vignette: A 13-year-old girl is undergoing hematologic evaluation. She is found to have a hemoglobin mutation that changes the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated to 20 mm Hg. In comparison, normal hemoglobin becomes 50% saturated with oxygen at 26 mm Hg. Which of the following sequelae is this patient most likely to develop as a result of her mutation?

clues.text: partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated to 20 mm Hg
clues.note: A P50 of 20 (below the normal 26) means hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly - a LEFT-shifted curve (increased oxygen affinity).

clues.text: normal hemoglobin becomes 50% saturated with oxygen at 26 mm Hg
clues.note: Normal P50 is ~26 mm Hg; a lower P50 indicates higher oxygen affinity (left shift), so less oxygen is unloaded to tissues.

whatMatters: A DECREASED P50 (20 vs normal 26) = HIGH-AFFINITY hemoglobin (LEFT-shifted curve). Hemoglobin binds oxygen tightly and UNLOADS less to peripheral tissues -> tissue hypoxia -> kidneys sense low O2 -> ↑erythropoietin -> compensatory ERYTHROCYTOSIS. Answer A.
strategy: Interpret P50: lower P50 = higher affinity = left shift = less O2 delivered to tissues. The body compensates for tissue hypoxia by making more red cells (EPO-driven erythrocytosis). Reject the hemolysis/fragility options (this is an affinity change, not membrane/oxidative damage: high-affinity hemoglobins are usually asymptomatic) and megaloblastic changes (B12/folate deficiency, unrelated).

eliminations.label: Hypoxia-induced hemolysis - sickle cell, not high-affinity Hb
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hemolysis triggered by deoxygenation, as in sickle cell disease (HbS polymerizes). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: high-affinity hemoglobins do not polymerize or hemolyze - they just release less O2; the compensatory response is erythrocytosis. ✅ Correct if: sickle cell disease (right-shifted, deoxy-triggered sickling).

eliminations.label: Increased osmotic fragility - hereditary spherocytosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: spherocytes lyse easily in hypotonic solution (membrane cytoskeleton defect: spectrin/ankyrin). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is a membrane disorder, not an oxygen-affinity change. ✅ Correct if: hereditary spherocytosis.

eliminations.label: Megaloblastic changes - B12/folate deficiency (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: large red cells from impaired DNA synthesis (vitamin B12/folate deficiency). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a nucleotide/DNA-synthesis problem, unrelated to a hemoglobin oxygen-affinity mutation. ✅ Correct if: macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils.

eliminations.label: Oxidant-induced hemolysis - G6PD deficiency
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hemolysis under oxidative stress (G6PD deficiency; Heinz bodies, bite cells). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: an affinity mutation doesn't cause oxidative hemolysis. ✅ Correct if: G6PD deficiency after antimalarials/fava beans/infection.

reasoning: P50 fell from 26 to 20 mm Hg = increased oxygen affinity = left-shifted curve
High-affinity hemoglobin unloads less oxygen to peripheral tissues -> tissue hypoxia
Kidneys sense hypoxia and increase erythropoietin -> more red cell production
mechanism: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve relates arterial PO2 to hemoglobin saturation; P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation, normally ~26 mm Hg) is the conventional measure of affinity. A DECREASED P50 (here 20 mm Hg) means INCREASED oxygen affinity - a LEFT-shifted curve - so hemoglobin binds oxygen more avidly and RELEASES less to the peripheral tissues (examples: high-affinity variants such as hemoglobins Chesapeake and Kempsey; also fetal hemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, and states with low 2,3-BPG, alkalosis, or hypothermia). The resulting relative tissue hypoxia is sensed by the kidneys, which increase ERYTHROPOIETIN secretion, stimulating the marrow to make more red cells - a compensatory ERYTHROCYTOSIS that restores oxygen delivery. Patients with high-affinity hemoglobins are therefore typically asymptomatic aside from a high hematocrit. This is not a hemolytic or membrane disorder: sickling/deoxy-triggered hemolysis (HbS), osmotic fragility (spherocytosis), oxidative hemolysis (G6PD deficiency), and megaloblastic changes (B12/folate) involve entirely different mechanisms.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Physio/Heme > oxygen-hemoglobin curve: ↓P50 = ↑affinity = left shift = less O2 to tissues; high-affinity hemoglobins -> tissue hypoxia -> ↑EPO -> erythrocytosis (usually asymptomatic).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Lower P50 = left shift = poor O2 unloading -> compensatory erythrocytosis (not hemolysis).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on P50, left vs right shift, oxygen affinity, 2,3-BPG, or erythropoietin? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Hemolysis options (sickle, spherocytosis, G6PD) and megaloblastic (B12/folate) are unrelated mechanisms - this is an affinity change.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: high-affinity Hb (low P50, left shift) -> tissue hypoxia -> ↑EPO -> erythrocytosis; usually asymptomatic.

keywords.back: Increased oxygen affinity (left shift), less O2 to tissues
↓2,3-BPG, alkalosis, hypothermia, fetal Hb, CO, methemoglobin, high-affinity variants

firstAid.detail: Physio: ↓P50 = left shift = ↑affinity -> less tissue O2 -> ↑EPO -> erythrocytosis.
Physio > left = fetal Hb/CO/methemoglobin/↓2,3-BPG; right = exercise/acidosis/↑2,3-BPG.

memoryHook: Greedy hemoglobin (low P50) won't let go of oxygen, so tissues go hungry; the kidney answers with EPO and the marrow makes extra red cells - erythrocytosis.
